commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor sources to module coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The classes sit in the default package, use `/* */` where Javadoc
belongs, and break the naming, import order and indentation rules. The
banner rows in Serangooner run past the 120 character hard limit, and
`delete` repeats the task number parsing that `updateStatus` already
does.

Let's move every class into a `serangooner` package, replace the old
headers with Javadoc, and bring the layout in line with the standard.
The repeated parsing moves into a single `parseTaskNumber` helper, so
the argument rules for `mark`, `unmark` and `delete` live in one place.

Program output is unchanged. Both the full command set and the argument
error paths were diffed against a build of the previous sources.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: CLAUDE.md: Replace pointer with full rules
commitResults.messageBody:
CLAUDE.md forwards to AGENTS.md, which frames the repository as a
generic starter template and gives the module conventions as bare links.
The commit format, the Java coding standard and the tagging workflow
have to be looked up mid-task, so they get missed.

Let's spell the rules out in CLAUDE.md: project facts, the commit
message convention, the se-education Java standard, the JUnit layout,
the tag-and-push steps, and the AI citation policy. AGENTS.md stays put
as the course's own file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add /done command for milestone release
commitResults.messageBody:
Closing an increment means compiling, reviewing the diff against the
standard, committing, tagging with the exact increment ID, then pushing
the commit and the tag as separate steps. Done by hand this invites a
missed step, and the standing rule against committing unasked has to be
waived each time.

Let's capture the sequence as a slash command taking the tag name as its
argument, mirroring the Codex skill in `.codex/skills/done`. Invoking it
counts as authorisation to commit and push, for that one milestone only.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-7: Save and load tasks from the hard disk
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks entered in one session are lost the moment Serangooner exits, so
the list must be rebuilt by hand on every run.

Let's persist the list to ./data/serangooner.txt, reading it when the
list is constructed and writing it back after every edit. TaskList owns
the Storage instance so the file cannot fall out of step with what the
user sees, and each task class encodes its own line so that adding a
task type later needs only one more override.

A line that cannot be understood is skipped and reported in a short
startup message rather than aborting the load, so one damaged line
never costs the user the rest of the list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Let each task type read its own saved line
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage both dispatches on the type code and works out where each
field sits, so the layout of a saved line is settled in two places
at once: the task class writes it, and Storage independently reads
it back. Storage also signals a bad line by throwing, which load()
catches purely to count it, even though a damaged line is expected
input rather than a fault.

Let's give each task type a fromSaveFields factory beside its
toSaveFormat, returning an empty optional when the line cannot be
read. Reading and writing then sit together in the class that owns
the format, Storage shrinks to a switch on the type code, and the
load path no longer uses exceptions for ordinary control flow.

A shared readSaveLine helper on Task holds the checks every type
makes, so a saved line is accepted only with the exact field count
expected. A description containing the field separator is therefore
reported as unreadable instead of being loaded back mangled.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-8: Store dates and times as date objects
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadlines and events hold their dates as raw text, so the bot cannot
tell a date from any other string handed to it. Nothing can be
compared or filtered, and whatever the user types is echoed straight
back.

Let's parse both into a TaskDateTime, which wraps a LocalDateTime and
remembers whether a time of day was given. Dates are read as
2019-10-15 or 2019-10-15 1800 and shown as 15 Oct 2019 or
20 Oct 2019, 6:00PM, while the save file keeps the input format so a
saved task reads back as the value that was written.

One class owns every formatter, so the two task types share a parser
instead of each growing its own. A date that no longer parses skips
its line on load, joining the unreadable lines the loader already
reports, so one stale date never costs the user the rest of the list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add command to view tasks on or between dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Dates are held as real dates, but the only way to find what falls on a
given day is to read the whole list by eye. A list that grows past a
screenful makes that impractical.

Let's add "on <date> [to <date>]", which lists the deadlines and
events falling on a single date or touching any date in a range.
Matching goes through Task.isWithin, so each task type decides for
itself what falling within a range means and the command never has to
test what type a task is.

Both listings share one renderer, and it numbers tasks by their
position in the full list, so a number read off a filtered view stays
usable with mark, unmark and delete.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject events that end before they start
commitResults.messageBody:
An event takes any two dates, so one running from 16 Oct to 14 Oct is
stored as written. That event can never be found again: matching looks
for a span running forwards, and a backwards span covers no day at
all, so it answers no date query.

Let's reject the pair when the end falls before the start, comparing
through TaskDateTime so a time of day counts as much as the date. A
saved event whose dates disagree is skipped on load, like any other
line the loader cannot make sense of.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
Extract user interactions into a Ui class
commitResults.messageBody:
The main method decorates the console, runs the command loop and
dispatches commands all at once, while TaskList composes the sentence
reporting what was read from the save file. The wording the user sees is
spread across two classes, and none of it can be exercised without a
real console.

Let's gather every console concern into a Ui class, and have TaskList
report load counts through a LoadReport record that Ui words. Ui takes
its streams through the constructor, so tests can drive it with piped
input and read back what it printed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Move task saving out of TaskList into main class
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList holds a Storage and writes the save file after every edit, so
a list of tasks cannot exist without a file behind it, and its test has
to create a temporary directory just to count tasks. The outcome of a
load is described twice over, by Storage.LoadResult and by
TaskList.LoadReport.

Let's hand TaskList a plain list of tasks and let Serangooner hold the
user interface, the list and the save file together, deciding when a
change is written back. Storage.LoadResult absorbs the error message so
that one class describes one file read.

Saving happens only after a command that can change the list, marked by
CommandType.isMutating. Saving after every command would rewrite the
file on a plain 'list' and destroy any line the load could not read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command parsing into a Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
Knowledge of how a command is written is spread across four classes:
TaskList slices arguments out of raw command strings, and Deadline and
Event each hold a private parser keyed to a hardcoded offset into the
keyword they belong to. Renaming a keyword means editing a task class,
a list class and the command enum together.

Let's gather every step that turns typed text into meaning into one
Parser class, which hands values to the rest of the program: a command
type, a task, a task number or a range of dates. TaskList takes those
values in place of command strings, so it no longer speaks command
syntax, and the tasks no longer know that a command exists. Offsets
now come from the keyword's own length and error messages from the
command's declared syntax, so a keyword can be reworded in one place.

Parser also trims the line it is given, which repairs a command typed
with a leading space; such a command used to lose a character off the
argument following its keyword.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Reduce TaskList to holding the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList carries nearly half the wording the program shows: every edit
returns a finished sentence, and the class renders both listings. Ui
claims in its own header to be the one place such wording lives, and a
list that answers in console prose cannot be handed to a different
kind of interface. The three add methods differ only by the label each
puts in its message.

Let's have every edit give back the task it touched and leave the
wording to Ui. A task now names its own kind, so a single add method
serves all three, and a listing comes back as tasks paired with the
numbers the user knows them by, which keeps a number read off a
filtered listing usable with mark, unmark and delete. The out of range
message stays behind, since the list alone knows its own size.

Drop MAX_TASKS as well. It named a limit that nothing enforced, being
only the initial capacity of the backing list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Task abstract
commitResults.messageBody:
A plain Task can be built, but it is not a whole task: it has no name
for its kind, falls on no date, and writes a save line carrying no type
code. Storage cannot read that line back, so such a task would vanish
on the next load without a word.

Let's make Task abstract, and getTypeName along with it, so that only
the kinds that answer those questions can exist. The constructor turns
protected to match. Nothing built a plain Task, so this closes the gap
before it is ever reached rather than fixing a fault.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add serialVersionUID to SerangoonerException
commitResults.messageBody:
Compiling with -Xlint:all warns that the class is serializable without
a version of its own, which is the last warning the build reports.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Ui the one owner of console output
commitResults.messageBody:
Two things sit on the wrong side of the line between showing something
and being something. CommandType builds the numbered help listing, the
last piece of user-facing rendering outside Ui, and the only reason Ui
still offers a method that prints a string handed to it. Ui in turn
runs afplay in a subprocess, so the class that speaks to the console
also depends on a macOS binary.

Let's have Ui render the help listing from the commands it is given,
which leaves CommandType holding command data alone, and let a
SoundPlayer own the noise, the file it comes from and the thread it
plays on. Ui keeps the decision to make a sound and knows nothing of
how one is made.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace the command switch with Command objects
commitResults.messageBody:
The main loop switches over a CommandType to decide what to do, then
asks the enum whether the list changed so that it knows to save. A new
command therefore means editing the enum, the switch and the parser
together, and the loop must know what each command needs in order to
call it at all.

Let's have Parser return a Command that already holds everything it
needs, and give every command an execute of its own. The loop reads a
line, runs whatever comes back, and asks only whether to stop. A
command that changes the list saves it, which leaves isMutating with
no one to ask, so it goes.

Saying goodbye is now a command like any other, so the divider that
closes the exchange comes from the loop and showFarewell no longer
draws one of its own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-MoreOOP'
Split classes into packages by responsibility
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class sits in one flat serangooner package, so the source layout
says nothing about which classes serve the user, which hold the model
and which touch the disk. It also hides the direction of dependencies.

Let's group them into command, storage, task and ui packages, leaving
the entry point, the parser and the shared exception at the root.
Dependencies then run one way: root to command, command to ui and
storage, both of those to task.

Two references stood against that order and are moved rather than
worked around. DateRange leaves Parser for the task package, so a
command no longer depends on the parser that built it. HelpCommand
words the command list itself and hands Ui plain strings, so ui no
longer depends on command. Storage reads saved tasks through
fromSaveFields, package-private and compiling only because every class
shared a package; it is now public, stating a dependency that was there
all along.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Packages'
Merge branch 'add-gradle-support'
Point Gradle at the Serangooner entry point
commitResults.messageBody:
The merged Gradle build carries the skeleton's names: it launches
seedu.duke.Duke and packages the fat JAR as duke.jar. Neither class
nor name exists here, so `gradle run` fails outright.

Let's set mainClass to serangooner.Serangooner and name the shadowJar
output serangooner.jar, so the build refers to the bot it actually
produces.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
